opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

Honestly, when I started at IIT Madras, I didn't arrive with a grand plan to work on AI. I was drawn to computer science broadly: I liked programming, I liked puzzles, and I liked the feeling of building something that actually worked. AI crept up on me over the course of the program.

What made it compelling was the gap between how easy things are for people and how hard they are for machines. You can read a paragraph, understand a joke, or follow instructions in a game without thinking about it. Then you try to get a computer to do even a small piece of that and realize how little we understand about what's going on. That gap felt like one of the most interesting open questions there was, and it sat right where computer science, math, linguistics, and even a bit of cognitive science meet.

The environment at IIT mattered too. You're surrounded by people who are very sharp and very curious, so you end up talking about ideas late into the night and pushing each other. And you get a strong grounding in fundamentals like algorithms, probability, and linear algebra. That foundation turned out to matter a lot later, because the field changed so quickly. The specific techniques I learned as an undergrad are mostly not what people use today, but the way of thinking carried over.

Language was the part that really hooked me. It's how we communicate, reason, and pass on knowledge. The idea that you could build systems that understand and use language, and maybe learn about the world through it, seemed both hugely ambitious and important. That curiosity is what eventually led me to graduate school and the research I've done since.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad interest in AI and language, but does not mention a Snake-bot competition in an introductory AI class or identify it as motivation to study AI more deeply.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, when I started at IIT Madras, I honestly didn't go in thinking "I'm going to do AI." I went in as a computer science undergrad like a lot of people do, drawn to the fact that computing was this general-purpose tool where you could build things and see them work almost immediately.

What pulled me toward AI specifically was a couple of things. One was the people. There were a few professors there working on machine learning and natural language, and this was back when NLP meant a lot of hand-built rules and statistical models, nothing like today. But I found the problems genuinely fascinating. Language is this incredibly messy, ambiguous thing that humans handle effortlessly, and the idea that you could get a computer to make sense of it felt almost audacious.

The other thing was that it sat at this intersection I really liked. It wasn't pure theory, where you prove things and that's the end of it, and it wasn't pure engineering either. You had to think about what intelligence even means, what it means to understand something, and then you had to actually build a system and test whether your idea held up. That loop of having an idea about cognition or language and then being able to falsify it with code was very compelling to me.

And I'd say the culture at IIT Madras mattered too. There was a lot of freedom to explore, and a lot of very driven peers. I did some early projects that, looking back, were pretty crude, but they got me hooked on the question of how machines can learn from data rather than being told exactly what to do. That question basically carried me through my PhD at MIT and everything since.

r001.rationale: The response discusses professors, NLP, AI’s theory-to-building loop, and early projects, but does not identify a Snake-bot competition in an introductory AI class as a motivating experience.

astra-6.text: What drew me in was the idea that you could build a system that learns to do something, rather than explicitly telling it every step to take. That felt like a fascinating computer science problem: how do you get from a program following rules to something that can adapt to a new situation? Language made that question especially interesting to me, because so much of how we communicate depends on context and knowledge that we leave unstated.

Language was especially interesting to me because it’s so natural for us, yet getting a machine to understand what someone means is surprisingly difficult. There was this combination of a very intuitive goal and some really challenging technical questions, and that made me want to explore it further.
